### Introduction

In this project I compare traffic stops in California and Washington using data from the Stanford Open Policing Project. I focus on three questions: (1) how the number of stops has changed over time in each state, (2) how often searches occur for different racial groups, and (3) whether searches for different racial groups are equally likely to find contraband (hit rates) in each state. All data wrangling is done using SQL; R is used only for visualization and formatting.

### Setup and SQL Connection



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#loading packages and connecting to SQL
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(DBI)
library(RMariaDB)

con_traffic <- dbConnect(
  RMariaDB::MariaDB(),
  dbname = "traffic",
  host = Sys.getenv("TRAFFIC_HOST"),
  user = Sys.getenv("TRAFFIC_USER"),
  password = Sys.getenv("TRAFFIC_PWD")
)

dbListTables(con_traffic)
```

### Analysis 1



::: {.cell output.var='stops_by_year_state'}

```{.sql .cell-code}

SELECT year, state, n_stops
FROM (
SELECT
YEAR(date) AS year,
'CA' AS state,
COUNT(*) AS n_stops
FROM ca_statewide_2023_01_26
WHERE date BETWEEN '2010-01-01' AND '2020-12-31'
GROUP BY YEAR(date)

UNION ALL

SELECT
YEAR(date) AS year,
'WA' AS state,
COUNT(*) AS n_stops
FROM wa_statewide_2020_04_01
WHERE date BETWEEN '2010-01-01' AND '2020-12-31'
GROUP BY YEAR(date)
) AS combined
ORDER BY year, state;

```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
stops_by_year_state |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = n_stops, color = state)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Traffic Stops Per Year: California vs Washington",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Number of Stops",
    color = "State")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](sql_traffic_stops_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



Overall, California has many more traffic stops than Washington each year. From 2010 to 2018, the number of stops in California decreases quite a bit, especially after 2014, while Washington’s numbers stay relatively stable with only small ups and downs. This suggests that either enforcement practices or driving patterns changed more in California than in Washington over this time period.

### Analysis 2



::: {.cell output.var='search_rate'}

```{.sql .cell-code}

SELECT
state,
subject_race,
COUNT(*) AS n_stops,
SUM(search_conducted) AS n_searches,
AVG(search_conducted) AS prop_searches
FROM (
SELECT subject_race, search_conducted, date, 'CA' AS state
FROM ca_statewide_2023_01_26

UNION ALL

SELECT subject_race, search_conducted, date, 'WA' AS state
FROM wa_statewide_2020_04_01
) AS combined
WHERE subject_race IS NOT NULL
AND date >= '2015-01-01'
GROUP BY state, subject_race
HAVING n_stops >= 500
ORDER BY state, prop_searches DESC;

```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
search_rate |>
  ggplot(aes(x = subject_race, y = prop_searches, fill = state)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Search Rate by Race (2015–Present)",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Proportion of Stops with Search",
    fill = "State")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](sql_traffic_stops_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



This figure shows the proportion of stops that involve a search by race for California and Washington since 2015. In both states, Black and Hispanic drivers are searched at higher rates than white and Asian/Pacific Islander drivers. Washington tends to have slightly higher search rates across most racial groups than California. These differences suggest that search practices are not experienced equally across racial groups or across states.

### Analysis 3



::: {.cell output.var='stops_month'}

```{.sql .cell-code}

SELECT
  state,
  MONTH(date) AS month,
  COUNT(*) AS n_stops
FROM (
  SELECT 'CA' AS state, date
  FROM ca_statewide_2023_01_26

  UNION ALL

  SELECT 'WA' AS state, date
  FROM wa_statewide_2020_04_01
) AS combined
WHERE date IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY state, month
ORDER BY month, state;

```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
stops_month |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = n_stops, color = state)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Traffic Stops by Month: CA vs WA",
    x = "Month of Year",
    y = "Number of Stops",
    color = "State"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](sql_traffic_stops_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



This plot compares the number of stops by month for California and Washington. Both states show more traffic stops in the summer months and fewer in the winter, but California has far more stops overall in every month. The similar seasonal pattern suggests that factors like weather, travel, or enforcement cycles affect both states in roughly the same way, even though the total volume of stops is very different.

### Conclusion

In this project, I used SQL to wrangle traffic stop data from California and Washington in order to compare patterns over time, across races, and across the calendar year. The first analysis showed that California has far more traffic stops than Washington, and that California’s stops declined substantially between 2010 and 2018 while Washington’s stayed relatively stable. The second analysis found that Black and Hispanic drivers are searched at higher rates than white and Asian/Pacific Islander drivers in both states, with Washington generally having slightly higher search rates overall. Finally, the third analysis showed that both states have more stops in summer and fewer in winter, suggesting similar seasonal dynamics despite very different total volumes. Together, these results illustrate how SQL can be used to explore large policing datasets and highlight differences in traffic stop practices across states and groups.

### Source

Data used in this project come from the Stanford Open Policing Project: <https://openpolicing.stanford.edu/data/>
